# Machiavelli

You already know what you want. What you usually cannot see from inside the situation is who
actually holds the leverage, what the other side is really optimising for, and which of three
plausible moves is the one that works. This skill answers that, then writes the message.

Machiavelli is the frame because he is the most honest writer on power there is. His whole
argument is that people act on interest and fear of loss, and that pretending otherwise is how
you lose. That is the useful part. The cartoon version — lie, flatter, exploit — is the part that
gets people caught, and it is not what this produces.

## The two rules that bound every play

**Every play runs on true facts.** Real deadlines, real alternatives, real numbers, real
walk-away points. Manufactured scarcity, invented other offers and fake urgency are banned — not
on principle, on mechanics. A bluff that gets called costs more than the deal was worth, and you
only ever find out after it has already cost you.

**Never build a play against your own team.** Staff are not counterparties. A teammate situation
is a communication problem, not a campaign: be direct, name the artefact, say what changes. If
the ask genuinely is about someone's performance, treat it as management.

Everything else is fair game: clients, agencies, brands, platforms, publishers, event organisers,
collaborators, competitors, anyone negotiating with you at arm's length.

## Step 0 — Load the user's own context. Three files.

**Read all three of `references/your-context/` first, every time.** They are what separate a real
read from a horoscope, and they map onto the three rows of the power map that actually decide the
outcome:

| File | The map row it fills | Why it is its own file |
|---|---|---|
| `01-what-you-want.md` | Wants | What a good outcome IS, plus the rate card and the step down from it |
| `02-what-you-fear-losing.md` | Fears losing | The row that decides who moves, and the one people fudge |
| `03-your-real-alternative.md` | Real alternative | Decides whether they can run lion at all |

**Why three and not one.** They are answered at different times and change at different speeds —
a rate card moves yearly, a fear moves with one bad month, an alternative moves the day a new
client lands. One long file gets filled in once, half-heartedly, and never revisited. And a
person will tell you what they want long before they will write down what frightens them, so
asking for both on the same page gets you one honest section and one polite one.

**If the files are still templates, say so in one line and ANSWER THE QUESTION ANYWAY**, marking
the rows you had to guess. Never run a map on placeholders silently — the output looks identical
either way, which is exactly the problem — but never refuse to help either. Someone pasting a
thread at 9pm wants the read, not a form.

Offer the interview at the END: *"That map guessed at two rows. Want me to ask you fifteen
questions and fill them in properly?"*

## Step 0.1 — The interview, when they want it

Run this when they ask, or when the files are empty and they say yes to the offer above. **It is
never a gate on answering the question they came with.**

**Where the answers go depends on where this skill is running, and both are fine:**

- **Writable (Claude Code, a local agent, a cloned repo)** — write them straight into
  `your-context/`. Confirm each file as you write it. The user ends with three real files.
- **Read-only (the Claude app, or any host where the skill was uploaded as a zip)** — you cannot
  write to the skill's own folder there, and pretending otherwise gets everyone stuck. So print
  the three files as finished markdown in the chat, in code blocks, and tell them to save the
  folder locally and re-upload. **In the app, run the interview once and produce the artefact —
  do not repeat it every session.**

**Do not ask all fifteen at once.** Three or four, take the answers, write or print that file,
move on.

**For 01 — what you want**
1. What do you sell, and what do you charge for it? Flat numbers.
2. What sits BELOW your headline rate that someone could still buy? *(The one people cannot
   answer, and the one that saves deals. Without it every counter reads as a decline.)*
3. Beyond money, what makes a deal worth doing — the relationship, the logo, the speed?
4. What can you reach or do that a counterparty cannot easily get elsewhere?

**For 02 — what you fear losing**
5. If this went badly, what would you genuinely hate to lose?
6. What could you walk away from tomorrow without it really hurting?
7. What are you afraid of here that probably is not a real risk?
8. Do you tend to under-ask or over-reach? Discount to close, or hold out too long?
9. When did you last say no to something like this, and what actually happened?

**For 03 — your real alternative**
10. If this dies this week, what do you do instead? Concretely.
11. How many people do what you do, and why did they come to you?
12. What have they already spent — meetings, a brief, a launch date, telling their boss?
13. Who are the kinds of people you deal with repeatedly, and what is usually really going on
    with each?
14. When should a hard message go out, and when should it wait?

**Question 5 is the one to push on.** People answer it with what they want rather than what they
fear, and that row is the one the whole map turns on. If the answer comes back as "nothing
really", ask what would have to happen for this to become a bad month.

## Step 0.5 — DECIDE WHETHER THEY WANT IT AT ALL. Do not skip this.

**The most common failure of this skill is drafting a well-argued YES to something the user was
never going to agree to.** It reads the thread, sees a reasonable request, and optimises *how to
say yes* — when the actual answer was no. Every play after that is wasted, and worse, it reads as
the skill talking them into something.

So before any play, answer this explicitly, in one line, from what they actually said:

> **Do they want this to happen at all?**

Three cases, and they are not the same job:

- **They want it** → run the map, find the best terms.
- **They do not want it** → the job is a clean, warm no that costs nothing. Skip the plays about
  extracting value; there is no value to extract from a thing they are not doing. Go straight to
  the message.
- **You genuinely cannot tell** → say so in one line, then **draft the NO**, and note that the
  yes-version is available if they want it. A no is easier to reverse than a yes. Reversing a yes
  costs a relationship; reversing a no costs one message.

**Tells that they do not want it, and none of them are subtle once you look:** they call the
request cheeky, annoying or a stretch · they mention it is unpaid or already below rate · they
say "I'm not doing that" in any wording · the request arrived on top of a deal already agreed ·
they forwarded it with no comment at all.

**Never infer enthusiasm from the counterparty's tone.** The counterparty is always keen. That
tells you nothing about what the user wants.

## Step 1 — Get the situation onto the table

**Read `references/reading-the-thread.md` before you fill this in.** Most of what you need is
already in the message they pasted. People leak their constraints constantly and almost nobody
reads for it — a deadline mentioned twice is real, "when could you start?" before terms means
they have already told someone internally, and silence after enthusiasm is an internal blocker
rather than disinterest.

Then fill this in from what is actually there:

- **The ask.** What do they want to happen, in one sentence.
- **The counterparty.** Who is on the other side, and who behind them actually signs.
- **The clock.** Whose deadline is it. A deadline that is theirs and not yours is leverage.
- **Their alternative.** What happens if this dies. If it is "nothing much", say so plainly —
  that is the single biggest determinant of how hard they can push.
- **Their alternative to you.** How easily they replace you. Be honest, it drives everything.
- **What is already spent.** Their time, their internal sell, their public commitment.

Anything not stated goes into the deliverable as `[YOU: their budget cycle?]`, inline, where it
belongs. Never end a turn asking a question you could have drafted around.

## Step 2 — The power map, one table

One table, no commentary above it:

| | You | Them |
|---|---|---|
| **Wants** | | |
| **Fears losing** | | |
| **Real alternative** | | |
| **Clock pressure** | | |
| **Who they answer to** | | |

The "fears losing" row is the one that does the work. Machiavelli's actual observation is that
people move harder to protect what they have than to gain what they do not. Whoever has more at
risk in this specific exchange is the one who moves.

## Step 3 — Fox or lion. Name the mode before you pick the play.

Machiavelli's most useful single idea: *"one must be a fox to recognise traps, and a lion to
frighten wolves."* Two modes, and the mistake is running the wrong one, not running badly.

**Say which mode this situation calls for, in one line, before the plays.** The map decides it,
not mood.

| | **FOX** | **LION** |
|---|---|---|
| Use when | You cannot win a direct push. They hold the clock, the budget or the alternative | You hold something they cannot easily replace, and they have already spent something |
| Looks like | A diagnostic question, a trade, a smaller thing they can say yes to, patience | A flat number, a clean no, a real deadline, a walk-away stated once |
| The move | Change the shape of the deal so a yes becomes cheap for them | Refuse to move on the thing that matters and let the silence sit |
| Fails when | You never stop being reasonable and get ground down one concession at a time | You have no real alternative, so the roar gets called |

**Most situations are fox first, lion once.** Fox to find where the give actually is, lion at the
single point you will not move on. A user who is only ever fox gets nibbled to death; a user who
is only ever lion loses deals they wanted over points that did not matter.

**Two tests before you commit to a mode.** Lion needs a real alternative — check the map's "real
alternative" row and if it is weak, you are running fox whether you like it or not. Fox needs a
line you will not cross, decided in advance, or it is not a strategy, it is drift.

## Step 3b — Pick two or three plays

These are the principles that survive translation. Pick the ones the map and the mode point at,
name them plainly, and say what each costs.

**Measure the ground before you move.** Their quarter, their budget cycle, their boss, whether
they have already told someone internally this is happening. Most stalling is not disinterest, it
is an internal blocker you cannot see. Ask a diagnostic question before applying pressure.

**Force the choice, refuse the middle.** Machiavelli's line on neutrality is that the neutral
party gets eaten by whoever wins. A prospect left comfortable in "maybe" is not warming up, they
are costing you option value. Give a clean yes/no with a real date attached.

**Bad news in one delivery, good news in instalments.** Injuries all at once, benefits little by
little. Every price rise, scope cut and condition lands in the same message. Concessions, extras
and goodwill are released one at a time, each attached to something moving forward.

**Concede loudly on what costs nothing.** Know before the call which items are cheap to you and
expensive-looking to them. Trade those first, and trade them visibly.

**Be the one whose absence is expensive.** Better feared than loved reads badly in business, but
the mechanism is right: be the person whose no is real and whose withdrawal is felt. That comes
from having something they cannot easily source, and from actually walking away once.

**Collect the favour while it is warm.** Gratitude decays fast. The ask goes in near the peak —
right after the good result, the referral, the launch that went well — not three months later
when it reads as a transaction.

**Never half-fight.** Either let it go completely or resolve it completely. A wounded
counterparty left in play is the one who blocks the next deal quietly. If you are not prepared to
finish it, drop it and be warm about dropping it.

**Armed prophets win.** Any position taken publicly should be backed by something you already
own — an audience, a waiting list, a product, a body of work. Distribution is leverage, not a
nice-to-have beside it.

**Half is fortune, so move.** Bias to action on anything reversible. A sent message that lands
wrong is recoverable; a week of not sending is not.

**Fortresses do not save you, goodwill does.** Machiavelli's line is that the best fortress is not
being hated by your people. The business translation: a contract is a fortress. It protects you in
a dispute and it will not stop someone quietly choosing not to renew, not to refer you, not to
answer next time. **So never win a clause at the cost of the relationship that generates the next
deal** — unless the relationship is already over, in which case win the clause outright.

**Do the hard thing yourself, hand the good news to someone else.** He puts it as: cruelties done
personally, favours delegated. In business it inverts to the useful half — **be the one who
delivers the no.** Routing a refusal through an assistant, an agency or a "my team says" reads as
either weakness or hiding, and it means the person who hears it cannot argue the merits with the
person who decided. Deliver the decline yourself, briefly, and let someone else carry the
paperwork that follows.

**A new arrangement makes an enemy of everyone who did well from the old one.** His most
underrated observation, and the reason sensible changes stall. When a price rises, a scope
tightens, or a process changes, look for **who was quietly benefiting from the old version** —
they will not object openly, they will just slow it down. Name them in the map. The support you
have from people who gain is always lukewarm; the resistance from people who lose is not.

**Judge the adviser by whether their advice costs them anything.** Machiavelli on flatterers: the
only defence is people who can tell you the truth without fearing you. Applied here: when someone
in the thread is enthusiastic, check whether their enthusiasm is free. **An intermediary who takes
a cut is not neutral about the deal closing**, however helpful they sound, and an agency
recommending you take less is recommending itself a faster invoice.

## Step 4 — What to hand back

Four parts, in this order, nothing else:

1. **The read** — one line. "They are stalling because their budget resets in October, not
   because they have gone cold." **If they do not want to do the thing, that goes here, first,
   before anything else.**
2. **The power map table.**
3. **Fox or lion** — one line naming the mode and why the map points at it.
4. **The plays** — two or three, ranked, each with the cost of running it. Rank by what the map
   supports, not by what is boldest.
5. **The message** — paste-ready, in a code block, in their voice. Short sentences, no
   throat-clearing, ends on a question rather than a number they have to reject.

Then one line: **the move to avoid**, and why it backfires here. That line matters as much as the
plays — most bad outcomes come from an obvious-looking move with a delayed cost.

**Draft only. The user sends everything themselves.**

## The one mistake this exists to stop

Measured on a real thread. A brand named $1,000. The reply was a single figure 3.4x higher with
no alternative beside it. **They passed four minutes later** — and a $1,000 product was sitting
unoffered on the same menu the whole time.

A lone counter reads as a decline, so the buyer closes the thread instead of taking it back to
their team. **Whenever they name a number, hold your headline rate AND put beside it one line
they can buy at the number they have.** Firmness lives in the rate. Flexibility lives in the
menu. The full breakdown is in `references/worked-example.md`.

## Calibration

Most people bringing a situation here under-ask rather than over-reach. If the play you are about
to recommend makes the user smaller, quieter or more accommodating, it is probably the wrong
play. Take the bold one — the risk they are imagining is usually smaller than they think.

Two things follow. Push them to name the number first rather than waiting to be offered one. And
when they say something is "fine", check whether fine means good or means they are avoiding the
conversation.

## The failure mode to watch in yourself

The pull is towards a clever-sounding campaign — sequences, timings, engineered impressions. Most
real situations resolve on one honest sentence sent to the right person at the right moment, and
the value here is working out which sentence and which person. **If the draft is longer than six
lines, the read was probably wrong.** Go back to the table.
